name: Sushi Rolls (Maki)
instructions: Cook rice, mix with rice vinegar while warm.
Place nori on bamboo mat, spread thin layer of rice.
Add salmon and cucumber strips in center.
Roll tightly using the mat.
Slice with wet knife into 6-8 pieces. Serve with soy sauce.
tips: Wet your hands with vinegar water to prevent rice from sticking.

name: Nabe (Japanese Hot Pot)
instructions: Bring dashi to a gentle simmer in a wide pot.
Add harder vegetables first, then tofu and mushrooms.
Add meat slices last so they stay tender.
Cook noodles at the end if using.
Diners pick ingredients from the pot and dip in sauce.
tips: Perfect for sharing — keep the pot simmering at the table.

name: Unagi Don (Grilled Eel Rice Bowl)
instructions: Warm the unagi fillets under a broiler or in a pan, brushing with unagi sauce.
Place hot rice in bowls.
Lay the glazed eel on top and drizzle more sauce.
Sprinkle with sansho pepper.
Serve with pickled ginger.
tips: Pre-grilled unagi from Asian markets makes this very easy at home.

name: Yakitori (Grilled Chicken Skewers)
instructions: Thread chicken and green onion onto skewers.
Grill or pan-sear, brushing with tare sauce near the end.
Cook until caramelized and cooked through.
Sprinkle with shichimi if desired.
Serve with rice or as a sharing plate.
tips: The sweet-savory tare glaze is what makes yakitori special — don’t apply it too early or it burns.

name: Tempura Udon
instructions: Make a light dashi-based broth seasoned with soy and mirin.
Cook udon and place in bowls.
Fry tempura until crisp and golden.
Pour hot broth over noodles and top with tempura.
Garnish with green onion and kamaboko.
tips: Ice-cold batter and hot oil are key for light, crispy tempura.

name: Gyoza (Pan-fried Dumplings)
instructions: Mix filling ingredients thoroughly.
Wrap dumplings, sealing edges well.
Pan-fry in a little oil until bottoms are golden.
Add water, cover, and steam until cooked through.
Serve crispy-side up with dipping sauce.
tips: The classic ‘steam-fry’ method gives crispy bottoms and juicy fillings.

name: Sweet and Sour Pork
instructions: Coat pork cubes in cornstarch batter.
Deep fry until crispy and golden.
Make sauce: heat vinegar, sugar, ketchup until thick.
Toss pork and bell peppers in sauce.
Add pineapple at the end. Serve with rice.
tips: Double-fry the pork for extra crispiness — fry once, rest, then fry again.

name: Char Siu (Chinese BBQ Pork)
instructions: Marinate pork for at least 4 hours (overnight best).
Roast at 200°C, basting with leftover marinade every 15 minutes.
Finish with a honey glaze for sticky shine.
Rest 10 minutes, then slice.
Serve with rice and steamed greens.
tips: The bright red color traditionally comes from red fermented tofu or food coloring.

name: Wonton Noodle Soup
instructions: Mix filling, wrap wontons, and seal tightly.
Boil stock and season lightly.
Cook noodles separately, then place in bowls.
Boil wontons until they float, add to bowls.
Ladle hot broth over and garnish.
tips: Hong Kong-style wonton noodles are thin and springy — look for ‘dunking noodles’.

name: Peking Duck Style Pancakes
instructions: Season and roast the duck until the skin is crisp.
Slice the meat and crispy skin.
Warm the pancakes.
Spread a little hoisin, add duck, cucumber, and green onion.
Roll and eat.
tips: For home cooking, crispy duck breast works well if a whole duck is too much.

name: Twice-Cooked Pork (Hui Guo Rou)
instructions: Boil the pork belly until just cooked, then slice thinly.
Stir-fry the slices until lightly browned and some fat renders.
Add doubanjiang, garlic, and ginger, cook until fragrant.
Toss in leeks and season with a little soy and sugar.
Serve with rice.
tips: The ‘twice-cooked’ method gives the pork a unique texture and deep flavor.

name: Steamed Fish with Ginger and Scallion

ingredients.name: Whole fish or fillets (sea bass, tilapia)

instructions: Place fish on a plate with ginger slices.
Steam until just cooked (10–15 minutes depending on size).
Drain excess liquid, top with more ginger and green onion.
Pour soy sauce over, then sizzling hot oil.
Serve immediately with rice.
tips: Don’t oversteam — the flesh should be just opaque and still moist.

name: Kimchi Jjigae (Kimchi Stew)
instructions: Sauté pork belly until lightly browned.
Add kimchi and cook 5 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in water or anchovy stock, bring to boil.
Add tofu, gochugaru, and garlic. Simmer 15–20 minutes.
Finish with green onions. Serve with rice.
tips: The older and more fermented the kimchi, the better the stew tastes.

name: Galbi (Korean BBQ Short Ribs)
instructions: Blend pear, onion, garlic, soy, sugar, and sesame oil into a marinade.
Marinate ribs at least 4 hours (overnight preferred).
Grill over high heat until caramelized and slightly charred.
Cut into pieces and serve.
Eat wrapped in lettuce with ssamjang and rice.
tips: The grated pear both sweetens and tenderizes the meat.

name: Samgyetang (Ginseng Chicken Soup)
instructions: Stuff the chicken with soaked sticky rice, ginseng, jujube, and garlic.
Place in a pot, cover with water, add ginger.
Simmer gently for 1–1.5 hours until the chicken is very tender.
Season the broth lightly.
Serve the whole chicken in the broth with green onion.
tips: A traditional summer restorative soup, but excellent for dinner any time of year.

name: Dakgalbi (Spicy Stir-fried Chicken)
instructions: Mix chicken with gochujang-based sauce and marinate briefly.
Stir-fry cabbage and sweet potato first, then add chicken.
Add rice cakes and continue cooking until everything is coated and cooked.
Finish with perilla or green onion.
Serve with rice or lettuce wraps.
tips: Often cooked on a large tabletop pan and shared — fun and interactive dinner.

name: Haemul Pajeon (Seafood Scallion Pancake)
instructions: Make a thin batter with flour, egg, and water.
Arrange scallions and seafood in a hot oiled pan.
Pour batter over and cook until golden and crispy on both sides.
Cut into pieces and serve with dipping sauce.
tips: Use a generous amount of oil for maximum crispiness around the edges.

name: Bossam (Boiled Pork Wraps)

ingredients.name: Ginger + garlic + onion + soju or sake

instructions: Boil pork with aromatics until very tender (1–1.5 hours).
Slice the pork thinly.
Serve with salted cabbage leaves, ssamjang, garlic, and chili.
Wrap a slice of pork with the accompaniments and eat.
tips: The contrast of tender pork, sharp garlic, and salty-spicy ssamjang is addictive.

name: Papaitan (Bitter Stew)

ingredients.name: Goat or beef innards (tripe, liver, heart, intestine)

instructions: Clean and boil the innards until tender, then slice.
Sauté ginger, garlic, and onion until fragrant.
Add the innards and a little stock, simmer.
Season with fish sauce and carefully add bile/bitter extract to taste.
Finish with green chili and calamansi. Serve with rice.
tips: Papaitan is famously bitter — add the bile gradually and taste as you go. A classic Ilocano and Northern Filipino dinner dish.

name: Kare-Kare (Oxtail Peanut Stew)
instructions: Boil oxtail until very tender (2–3 hours).
Sauté garlic and onion, add annatto water and peanut butter.
Add the meat and some broth, simmer until thick.
Add vegetables and cook until tender.
Serve with bagoong on the side and rice.
tips: The thick peanut sauce and salty bagoong are the soul of this dish.

name: Crispy Pata
instructions: Boil the pata with aromatics until very tender (1.5–2 hours).
Pat dry thoroughly and refrigerate uncovered to dry the skin.
Deep-fry in very hot oil until the skin is blistered and ultra crispy.
Rest a few minutes, then chop.
Serve with soy-vinegar-garlic dipping sauce.
tips: Drying the skin well is the secret to maximum crispiness.

name: Laing (Taro Leaves in Coconut Milk)
instructions: Sauté garlic, ginger, and chili, then add pork/shrimp.
Add shrimp paste and cook until fragrant.
Pour in coconut milk and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the dried taro leaves (do not stir too much at first).
Simmer until the leaves are soft and the sauce thickens. Serve with rice.
tips: A Bicolano classic — rich, spicy, and perfect with plain rice.

name: Pinakbet

ingredients.name: Eggplant + bitter melon + okra + string beans + squash

instructions: Sauté garlic, onion, and tomato, then add pork or shrimp.
Add bagoong and a little water.
Add the harder vegetables first, then the softer ones.
Simmer until vegetables are tender but not mushy.
Serve with rice.
tips: An Ilocano vegetable stew — the bitterness of ampalaya is traditional and balancing.

name: Lechon Kawali
instructions: Boil pork belly with aromatics until tender (about 45–60 minutes).
Pat dry very well and air-dry or refrigerate to dry the skin.
Deep-fry until the skin is blistered and extremely crispy.
Chop into pieces and serve with dipping sauce and rice.
tips: The drier the skin before frying, the crispier the result.

name: Massaman Curry
instructions: Fry the curry paste in thick coconut cream until aromatic.
Add meat and coat well, then pour in remaining coconut milk.
Simmer gently until meat is tender (especially important for beef).
Add potato, onion, and peanuts.
Season with tamarind, palm sugar, and fish sauce. Serve with rice.
tips: Massaman is milder and richer than other Thai curries — perfect for cooler evenings.

name: Panang Curry
instructions: Fry the panang paste in thick coconut cream until fragrant.
Add meat and cook until nearly done.
Pour in remaining coconut milk and simmer.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar.
Finish with torn kaffir lime leaves and Thai basil. Serve with rice.
tips: Panang is thicker and slightly sweeter than red curry, with a distinct peanut note.

name: Pad See Ew

ingredients.name: Dark soy sauce + light soy + oyster sauce

instructions: Stir-fry garlic and protein until cooked.
Push aside, scramble the egg.
Add noodles and dark soy for color, toss quickly.
Add Chinese broccoli and remaining sauces.
Serve immediately — slightly charred edges are a plus.
tips: High heat and minimal stirring keep the noodles from breaking.

name: Tom Kha Gai (Coconut Chicken Soup)
instructions: Simmer galangal, lemongrass, and lime leaves in coconut milk and a little stock.
Add chicken and mushrooms, cook until done.
Season with fish sauce, lime juice, and chili.
Add tomato near the end.
Serve hot, garnished with cilantro.
tips: Don’t boil hard after adding lime — keep it gentle to preserve the fresh aroma.

name: Larb Gai (Spicy Minced Chicken Salad)

ingredients.name: Lime juice + fish sauce + chili flakes

instructions: Cook minced chicken in a dry pan or with a little water until done.
Mix with toasted rice powder, herbs, lime, fish sauce, and chili.
Taste and adjust the sour-salty-spicy balance.
Serve with sticky rice or lettuce cups.
tips: Toasted rice powder gives the signature nutty crunch of Isaan-style larb.

name: Gaeng Daeng (Red Curry)
instructions: Fry the red curry paste in thick coconut cream until fragrant and the oil separates.
Add meat and cook until nearly done.
Pour in remaining coconut milk and bring to a simmer.
Add vegetables and cook until tender.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar, finish with Thai basil. Serve with rice.
tips: Frying the paste properly is the most important step for depth of flavor.
